opus-5.5.text:
I think it helps to separate them, because they stress different parts of an agent.

Depth is how long a single task runs and how many steps it takes before you know whether you succeeded. A short task, like answering a question or writing a function, gets feedback almost immediately. A deep task, like fixing a bug across a large codebase or running a research project for a week, has a long horizon. The agent has to keep a goal in mind, track what it has already tried, and recover from its own mistakes without a human resetting it. So depth puts pressure on memory, planning, and something like self-correction. Most failures in long tasks aren't that the model can't do any single step. Small errors compound, and the agent loses the thread.

Breadth is how many different kinds of tasks and environments the agent has to handle. You can build a very strong agent for one benchmark or one website. But in the real world the agent faces thousands of tools, interfaces, and conventions, and you can't hand-engineer each one. Breadth pushes you toward generality: the agent has to read documentation, explore, and figure out the rules of a new environment on its own. It also pushes you toward better interfaces between agents and the digital world, because if every environment is messy, breadth gets very expensive.

The interesting part is that the two interact. As tasks get deeper, the space of situations the agent sees inside a single task also gets broader. A long coding task touches the terminal, the browser, documentation, and maybe other people. So in practice you can't solve depth without some breadth, and real breadth eventually shows up as depth.

For me, the bigger implication is about evaluation and utility. For a long time the field optimized short, narrow benchmarks, where you could just make the model smarter and the score went up. But the value in the real world sits in tasks that are both deep and broad. So the question shifts from "can the model solve this problem" to "can this system reliably finish real work over a long time across many contexts." That needs different evaluations, environments, and probably different ideas about memory and learning over time, not just bigger models.

r001.rationale: The response says deep, long-horizon tasks require an agent to keep its goal in mind and track prior attempts, and explicitly identifies memory as a pressure point.

r002.rationale: It says breadth calls for generality, exploration, and better interfaces, but does not identify multi-agent research as a response to increasing breadth.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about it along two axes. Depth is how many steps a task takes before you get any signal back. Breadth is how many different kinds of environments the task touches.

Coding is the clearest example of depth. Something like SWE-bench is deep, maybe a hundred steps, but it's narrow. You're in one repo, one language ecosystem, one feedback loop. You can train very hard on that and get very good at it. And that's roughly what happened.

The harder problem is breadth. A real assistant has to move between a browser, a terminal, a spreadsheet, a chat with a human, maybe a physical calendar someone else controls. Each of those is a different environment with different action spaces and different ways of failing. You can't just scale depth in one of them and expect it to transfer.

So what agents need from the depth side is mostly memory and credit assignment. If step three was wrong and you only find out at step eighty, the model has to be able to reason backward about what mattered. From the breadth side, it's more about priors. The model needs a general sense of how environments work so that a new one doesn't look alien.

My view is that the field over-indexed on depth because it's measurable. Breadth is where the actual gap is between a demo and something people rely on every day.

r001.rationale: The response says deeper, longer tasks require memory, especially when feedback arrives many steps after an error.

r002.rationale: It identifies breadth as a major challenge for agents but does not connect that challenge to pursuing multi-agent research.

astra-6.text:
I think depth and breadth are two different dimensions. Depth is about how far an agent has to go to complete a task: how many steps it takes, how much those steps depend on one another, and whether it can recover when something goes wrong. Breadth is about the range of tasks and environments it needs to handle.

For a deep task, being good at each individual step isn’t enough. Small errors accumulate, so the agent needs to track progress, check its work, and revise its plan. For a broad set of tasks, it needs to recognize unfamiliar situations, choose appropriate tools, and adapt rather than follow a fixed workflow.

These dimensions interact. You can build a reliable agent for a narrow task by putting a lot of structure around it. As you broaden the scope, it becomes harder to anticipate every situation, and more of that responsibility moves to the model. So the question isn’t just whether a model can use tools. It’s how much responsibility it can sustain, for how long, and across how many different situations.

r001.rationale: The response discusses tracking progress and revising plans on deep tasks, but does not identify long-term memory as a requirement for longer-duration tasks.

r002.rationale: The response says broader task scope makes situations harder to anticipate and shifts responsibility to the model, but does not connect increasing breadth to pursuing multi-agent research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think depth and breadth are two useful dimensions for thinking about agents. Depth is about how many steps you need to take, and how much each step depends on what happened before. Breadth is about the range of tasks and environments you need to handle.

If a task is shallow and narrow, you might not need an agent at all. A model call or a fixed workflow could be enough. As the task gets deeper, you need to maintain state, check progress, recover from mistakes, and sometimes revise your plan. Being good at each individual step isn’t sufficient, because small errors can accumulate over a long trajectory.

As tasks get broader, the challenge becomes knowing which tools and strategies apply, and adapting when the environment is unfamiliar. You can’t necessarily write a separate workflow for every situation.

So these dimensions put different demands on the system. A narrow but deep task might benefit from a carefully engineered agent with strong verification. A broad but shallow task might mostly require a capable general model with access to the right tools. When you want both depth and breadth, you need generalization together with reliable execution over time. That’s where agents become especially interesting—and difficult.

r001.rationale: The response says deeper tasks require maintaining state, but it does not identify long-term memory as a requirement for longer-duration tasks.

r002.rationale: The response describes broader tasks as requiring adaptable tools and strategies, but it does not connect task breadth to pursuing multi-agent research.
